name: Oliver Cromwell
role: English general and Lord Protector of England, Scotland and Ireland (1653-1658)
summary: A Parliamentary army commander who defeated the King in the Civil War and governed as Lord Protector under the Instrument of Government. He favoured liberty of conscience for Protestant sects but not for Catholics or bishops, opposed a wide franchise, ran the Major-General system of rule and the conquests of Ireland and Scotland, and refused the crown in 1657.

notes:
Nulls mark topics with no recorded statement in the sources used: Jews (readmission and their status) and Catholic civil rights beyond the Mass and the franchise are not addressed in the letters and speeches read. His kingship view is taken from the 1657 debates, where he refused the title but accepted that the Instrument could be amended. The Putney property remarks quoted in the record are mostly Ireton's and Rainborough's, not Cromwell's, and are not counted. Carlyle's commentary is treated as narration, not Cromwell's words, except where quoted as his speech.

Merged with an independent gpt-6.1-sol audit: 27 answers taken from it, 21 agreed, 3 conflicts settled by the integrator.

gpt-6.1-sol notes: Independent pass; the existing audit was consulted only for its notes and bibliography. Downloaded and searched the Cromwell Association’s complete Carlyle collection of 19 speeches and 205 letters, separating Cromwell’s words from editorial commentary. Source numbering and some dates in the site index are inconsistent; identify passages by speech contents and PDF titles. All 490 statements reviewed; modern economic doctrines were not assigned from a mercantilist or Puritan label. Of the ten priority questions only equal-outcomes receives a stated answer: explicit opposition to levelling fortunes. Restrictions on trade and an exclusive company monopoly do not establish a theory of profit, production for use or public industrial ownership. No direct ecology or technology position located. Protestant toleration and Jewish readmission do not erase explicit restrictions on Catholic worship. The record of coups and exclusions qualifies constitutional rhetoric. Historical inferences are individually marked. Diplomatic support for the Piedmont Protestants does not establish a position on humanitarian military intervention, which remains null.
